questions.title: How a lysosome resists its own enzymes
questions.question: Lysosomes resist digestion by their own hydrolytic enzymes due to presence of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lysosome is bounded by a single unit (bilayer) membrane like other cytoplasmic membranes, not by a monolayer, and a monolayer is not the protective feature being tested here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A pH of 7.2 is roughly neutral/cytosolic, not the acidic lysosomal environment, and pH alone is not the membrane-protection mechanism being asked about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipopolysaccharide is a bacterial cell-wall component, not a feature of the mammalian lysosomal membrane.
explanations.D: Correct. The lysosomal membrane resists its own hydrolytic enzymes through unusual phospholipid content together with highly glycosylated membrane proteins, which present a protective sugar coat on the luminal face that shields the membrane proteins from the very enzymes the lysosome contains. This structural, membrane-based protection is why the lysosome can hold active digestive enzymes without digesting itself. It is a commonly tested cell-biology mechanism distinguishing structural protection from any idea that the enzymes are simply too weak to act on their own membrane.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lysosomal proton pumps are active, not inactive — they actively transport hydrogen ions into the lumen to keep it acidic, which is a different mechanism (enzyme activation) from membrane self-protection.

questions.learning_objective: Explain how the lysosomal membrane protects itself from digestion by its own hydrolytic enzymes.

questions.title: Optimal pH for lysosomal enzyme activity
questions.question: Lysosomal enzymes are active at which of the following pH?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A pH of 4 is more acidic than the lysosomal lumen's typical working range and is not the value given for hydrolase activity here.
explanations.B: Correct. Lysosomal proton pumps transport hydrogen ions into the lumen, creating a low, acidic medium — around pH 5 — that is the condition needed to activate the lysosome's hydrolytic enzymes. Outside this acidic range the same hydrolases are far less active, which both protects the neutral-pH cytosol if a lysosome should leak and confines effective digestion to the lysosomal compartment itself. This pairing of proton-pump acidification with hydrolase activation is a core, frequently tested lysosome fact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A pH of 6 is closer to neutral than the acidic optimum described for lysosomal hydrolase activity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A pH of 7 is essentially neutral, the cytosolic pH the lysosome's acidic lumen is specifically distinguished from.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A pH of 8 is alkaline, the opposite direction from the acidic lysosomal lumen.

questions.learning_objective: State the acidic pH at which lysosomal hydrolytic enzymes are active.
